open_questions: Will the organization prefer a specific behavioral framework or a general approach?

devices.what: An angular desk calendar that holds concrete tally marks instead of vague complaints
A wide whiteboard tracking events from past errors to future collaborative plans
A visual thread between the manager and colleague that strains or heals
A thick, hand-drawn red marker stroke that aggressively crosses out absolute words
A torn paper wipe that reveals the objective truth beneath subjective layers

concept: Visualizing the contrast between abstract personality criticism, which is messy and subjective, and concrete observable behavior, which is clean, structured, and objective.

value_script.why: A pale open establishing the awkward baseline without heavy contrast
A dark break for the key mechanism of observable behavior, bringing sharp focus
A slightly richer middle as we map objective business impacts
A lift at the close for the collaborative payoff and clear future path

alternatives: round friendly shapes instead of angular
traditional slide joins instead of material torn paper joins
world: A stylized office environment that acts as an infinite whiteboard stage, allowing the camera to push seamlessly from messy interpersonal moments into clean, objective structures.

beats.intent: Split screen of manager and colleague, negative attitude in a chat bubble
beats.line: Picture a manager pulling a colleague aside. She calls his negative attitude a problem.

beats.intent: Colleague crosses arms; red jagged line connects them
beats.line: He gets defensive immediately. The relationship strains. The actual work never improves.
You know that giving feedback feels personal. It feels awkward.
beats.intent: Presenter beside personal and awkward text
Presenter gestures to a sharp focus bracket that clears the words
beats.line: Why does it always feel so difficult? A simple shift in focus fixes that.
Look at the phrase negative attitude. It is a personality trait. Critiquing a personality trait provokes defensiveness. It prevents constructive conversation.
beats.intent: Motion: phrase slides into a red box labeled personality trait that pulses
Manager points to tally calendar showing 3 distinct marks
beats.line: Watch what happens when she says something else. She points out he interrupted three times.

beats.intent: Camera lens frame overlays the tally marks
beats.line: That has a name, it is called observable behavior. Observable behavior is specific actions or words. A video camera could capture it.
Here is where people slip. It is not absolute. It is specific.
beats.intent: Absolute vs Specific text on angular ribbon labels
Motion: always and never crossed out with thick red marker
beats.line: Using absolute words makes feedback less accurate. Words like always or never. Why is that bad? They can easily reject it.

beats.intent: Thought bubble pops, leaving only concrete tally marks
beats.line: Replacing abstract personality labels with observable actions helps. It removes subjective guesses about internal motives.

beats.intent: Pocket rule card lands
beats.line: The pocket rule. Critique the action, not the person.
Now you, which statement targets observable behavior? Option A, you never seem to care. Option B, you submitted it late. Pause, and decide.
beats.intent: Two options in bare panels
Option B highlights green; never glows red
beats.line: The correct answer is B. You submitted the report two days after the deadline. The wrong answer uses the word never. It assumes they do not care.

sections.world: A stylized office environment that acts as an infinite whiteboard stage
sections.treatment: story-cartoon, flat fills, big-headed outlined people with chat bubbles on a warm paper ground
sections.accent_on: The specific words or tally marks (green) vs the subjective personality labels (red)

beats.intent: Meeting room; colleague sits under floating tally marks
beats.line: Say the colleague interrupted three times. During the client pitch.

beats.intent: Large duotone question mark icon beside the table
beats.line: You just named the behavior. Why does it matter?
You need to connect it to an outcome. A complete feedback statement links the observed behavior. It links directly to its objective impact. The impact on the task or team.
beats.intent: Arrow connects tally marks to an objective impact bare panel
Clock graphic showing 10-minute segment subtracted
beats.line: So she tells him, we lost ten minutes. Ten minutes of presentation time.

beats.intent: Colleague nods at objective timeline, uncrossed arms
beats.line: Explaining the business impact helps the recipient. They see the objective consequences of their behavior. They do not feel personally attacked.
Here is where people slip. It is not an emotional disaster. It is strictly factual.
beats.intent: Motion: theatrical face crossed out, replaced by clean graph
Graph lines adjust to a moderate dip instead of catastrophic plunge
beats.line: Impact statements must remain strictly factual. Do not exaggerate emotional distress.

beats.intent: Metallic shield stamp guards the relationship line
beats.line: People assume any negative feedback ruins relationships. They avoid it to protect feelings. But objective facts protect feelings.

beats.intent: Pocket rule card lands
beats.line: The pocket rule. State the behavior and its business impact.

beats.intent: Motion: feedback statement splits into two distinct halves
beats.line: Now you, identify the parts. You missed the deadline, so we lost the client. Which part is the impact? Pause, and point to it.
The impact is losing the client. Missing the deadline is the observable behavior. It connects the action to a consequence.
beats.intent: Lost the client highlights blue as objective impact
Silhouette of colleague leaving; empty brackets below
beats.line: Try one more. A colleague leaves early every day. How do you frame the feedback? Pause, and build a statement.

beats.intent: Brackets fill: concrete behavior on left, factual impact on right
beats.line: You start with the specific action. You left at four o'clock twice this week. Then you state the objective impact. I had to finish the report alone.

sections.world: A meeting room that fades away to leave only the objective timeline board
sections.accent_on: The objective consequences (blue arrows and clock segments)
sections.treatment: story-cartoon, shifting to cleaner bare panels and duotone icons to reflect objectivity
story-cartoon, bright, energetic grain textures with collaborative drawing motions

beats.line: The feedback is delivered. Now what?
beats.intent: Manager and colleague at the timeline board

beats.line: You might want to rehash the meeting. Dwelling entirely on past errors traps the conversation. It traps it in an unproductive argument.
beats.intent: Heavy circular arrow traps figures in an endless loop on past dates

beats.line: A brief mention of the past event is necessary. It grounds the conversation.
beats.intent: Heavy loop breaks into just one small anchor dot

beats.line: But then you need to pivot. How do you fix the next pitch?
beats.intent: Bright arrow extends timeline to future calendar date
Motion: drawing an upward trajectory arrow on the board
beats.line: Shifting the focus to future actions works. It turns a difficult critique into a planning session. A collaborative planning session.

beats.intent: Clean speech bubble from manager displays question
beats.line: So she asks, how can we approach this? How can we approach the next project?

beats.intent: Colleague draws the final step of the plan
beats.line: Asking the recipient to propose a different approach helps. It builds ownership of the new behavior.
The conversation ends. The relationship stays intact. The work actually improves this time.
beats.intent: Red jagged line morphs into a healthy green handshake stamp

beats.line: The pocket rule. Ask them to plan the next step.
beats.intent: Presenter with pocket rule card

sections.accent_on: The bright forward-pointing arrow and green handshake
sections.world: The same timeline board, now fully open and stretching into the right-hand future space
